1387.title: Lourdes and Fatima as pilgrims
1387.hook: the sick and their caregivers at the heart of the pilgrimage
1387.howItsDone: Dioceses and parishes organize pilgrimages to Lourdes and Fatima that bring sick people together with volunteer caregivers, nurses and doctors; the sick are seated first at Masses and processions and are prayed for and blessed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy Land, the ground some call the fifth gospel, and everyone who lives on it. Your line was the fifth gospel.

Evening at Lourdes, in the south of France. A procession is forming, and candles are being lit all across the square. At the very front, before the bishops and the choirs, come the wheelchairs. Old men in blankets. A girl with a breathing tube. A woman on a stretcher, looking up at the sky. Pushing them are volunteers, some of them teenagers, some doctors on vacation, some who were pushed in a chair themselves years ago. The crowd waits. Nobody hurries them. At a shrine famous for hoped-for cures, what stands out is the order of the line.
screen: `CANDLES AT LOURDES.` → `WHEELCHAIRS AT THE FRONT.` → `VOLUNTEERS PUSHING.`

segments.voice: Lourdes in France and Fatima in Portugal are shrines tied to appearances of Mary that the Church has judged worthy of belief. Earlier on this path, you met them as stories. Today, meet them as pilgrims do. At Lourdes, the sick get the places of honor: seated at the front for Mass and processions, with the Eucharist carried past them in blessing. Volunteers come from parishes and dioceses to push chairs, carry stretchers, help at the baths and serve meals, some year after year. Why? In Matthew's Gospel, describing the judgment of the nations, Jesus lists what the blessed did for him, including, in the Douay-Rheims, "sick, and you visited me." At these shrines, Catholics act that verse out in public, with the whole crowd watching. What about cures? Some pilgrims hope for healing, and the Church takes reports seriously. At Lourdes a medical office examines claims, and the Church is slow and careful before calling any cure a miracle. Some pilgrims speak of a different healing: peace, courage, a family reconciled, a caregiver who finally rests. At Fatima, some pilgrims walk long distances to the shrine, pray the rosary together in different languages, and fill the square with candles at night. The sick are prayed for by name. The two differ in their stories. As pilgrimages, they share a center: the weakest go first, and the strong push.

1388.title: Your local shrine
1388.hook: a shrine may be closer than you think
1388.howItsDone: Catholics visit diocesan and national shrines near home for a day of prayer, Mass and confession; dioceses and parishes list approved shrines and sometimes organize local pilgrimages to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lourdes and Fatima as pilgrims, where wheelchairs lead the procession and volunteers push. Your line was the sick go first.

Forty minutes up the highway, past a gas station and a feed store, a small brown sign marks a turnoff. A gravel road. A grotto made of fieldstone, with a statue of Mary and rows of candles in red glass. A rack of rosaries left by people who prayed and went home. On a weekday afternoon, a retired couple sits on a bench, a man in work boots kneels on the gravel, and a woman reads the handwritten notes tucked into the stones. None of them flew anywhere. Some drove past it for years before stopping.

segments.voice: First, what a shrine is. The Church's Code of Canon Law defines one simply: a church or other sacred place that the faithful visit on pilgrimage for a particular reason of devotion, with the local bishop's approval. So a shrine is measured not by size or fame but by prayer: people come on purpose. Then, the oldest pattern. In Genesis, Jacob is running from his brother. He stops for the night at an ordinary spot, puts a stone under his head, and dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven. He wakes and says, in effect, the Lord was in this place and I didn't know it. He calls it the house of God, then sets the stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. He didn't travel to a famous holy site. He found one on the road he was already on. Why do local shrines matter? A grand pilgrimage may come once in a lifetime, and some people can never make one: too sick, too poor, too busy caring for someone. A shrine a drive or a bus ride away is a pilgrimage for the rest of us. It can hold a grandparent's devotion, a parish's history, an immigrant community's patron saint, brought from home. Your diocese's website or parish office can tell you which shrines are near. Some sit beside a big church; some are a single statue at the edge of a cemetery. The pilgrimage can be an afternoon, and the prayer the same.

1389.title: Incorruptibles, honestly
1389.hook: some saints' bodies decay less than expected; the Church does not treat this as proof
1389.howItsDone: Catholics venerate the relics of saints, including some whose bodies are displayed in churches; the Church does not treat a body's preservation as a miracle or as evidence in canonization, which looks at heroic virtue and miracles attributed to the saint's intercession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your local shrine: a grotto off the highway, and Jacob waking on a stone pillow to find the Lord was in that place. Your line was close to home.

A glass case in a side chapel. Inside, a nun lies as if asleep, hands folded, face calm. A sign says she died long ago. Tourists lean in close. One whispers that it's a miracle. Another whispers that it must be wax. A child asks, loudly, whether she's real. Nobody quite knows what to say. Here's what neither whisperer may expect: the Catholic Church doesn't count this as proof of anything. Not of holiness, not of a miracle, not of the faith.
screen: `A NUN IN A GLASS CASE.` → `MIRACLE, OR WAX?` → `THE CHURCH SAYS: NOT PROOF.`

segments.voice: Incorruptibles is the name people give to saints whose bodies, when their tombs were opened, had decayed less than expected. The word sounds like a perfect body; the honest picture is often different. Some are dried, darkened or partly preserved, and some on display have faces and hands covered with wax or a mask, which some shrines say openly when asked. Next, what the Church does with it. Investigating a candidate for sainthood, it looks at a life of heroic virtue and at miracles attributed to the person's prayers after death, such as healings doctors cannot explain. A preserved body isn't on that list. Saints' remains have also decayed in the ordinary way, and that counts against no one. So the Church's posture is careful: interesting, worth studying, not proof. Then, why honor the remains at all. The body matters in Catholic belief. Paul writes of the resurrection of the dead, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption." The hope isn't a body that stays fresh in a glass case. It's that God raises the dead, whatever state the tomb is in. A decayed saint and a preserved saint share the same promise. Last, honesty itself. Some cases have natural explanations: dry air, the burial place, embalming. Some are still debated. A Catholic is free to say, calmly, we don't know. Faith that needed a perfect corpse to stand up would be fragile, and the Church doesn't ask anyone to lean on it.

1390.title: Votive candles
1390.hook: a candle left burning keeps praying after you leave
1390.howItsDone: Catholics light votive candles in churches before images of Christ, Mary and the saints, often leaving a small offering, and pray for a particular person or intention; some keep a candle at a home altar.

A nurse finishes a night shift and stops at a church that's open early. Near a statue of Mary stands a metal rack of little candles in glass cups, some burning, some burned out. She drops a few coins in the slot, takes a long match, and lights one. She kneels for maybe a minute, thinking of a patient, a man with no visitors. Then she has to go: sleep, kids, life. But the little flame stays. It burns all morning while she sleeps, beside others someone lit for a mother, a soldier, a baby, an exam.

segments.voice: A votive candle is lit as a sign of a prayer, for someone or something specific, and left to burn before an image of Christ, Mary or a saint. In your first month, you learned why there's fire in every church. Here's the root. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." So when Catholics light a candle, it isn't decoration. It points to him. Next, what the candle does, and doesn't. A candle isn't a prayer machine. It doesn't pray instead of you, and a bigger candle doesn't get a better answer. It's a sign: you came, you prayed, and you left something behind that says so. The prayer was yours; the flame keeps it in view after you've gone back to work. Then, the coins. The slot is for an offering, which helps pay for the candles and the church. It isn't a price; the prayer never depended on the coins. Who's it for? Anyone. A Catholic can light a candle for a friend of another faith, or of none, for an enemy, for someone who died long ago, for a person on the news whose name they'll never know. The candle doesn't check credentials. Last, what it teaches: prayer doesn't end when you stand up. The Catholic imagination keeps finding small ways to say that, a candle, a medal, a holy water font by the door, each one a reminder you can see.

1391.title: Grace before meals
1391.hook: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts
1391.howItsDone: Catholic families make the sign of the cross and say the traditional grace, "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," together before meals at home and sometimes in restaurants; some also say a grace after meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, votive candles: a nurse lighting one after a night shift, and a flame that stays when she goes. Your line was the candle keeps praying.

Tuesday night. Spaghetti, again. A seven-year-old has his fork halfway to his mouth when his grandmother clears her throat. He freezes, puts the fork down, and sighs. Everyone makes the sign of the cross, some faster than others. Then, together, in about the time it takes the steam to rise off the plates, they say it. Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen. Fork back up. Someone asks for the parmesan. It's over so fast it's easy to miss what was just said.
screen: `A FORK HALFWAY UP.` → `A GRANDMOTHER CLEARS HER THROAT.` → `SAID IN THE TIME STEAM RISES.`

segments.voice: That's the table grace in a traditional English form. You met it in your second week, at a grandmother's table. Today, slowly: four short phrases. First, bless us. Not the food first. The people: the ones at the table, tired, hungry, maybe annoyed with each other. Second, these thy gifts. The spaghetti was bought at a store, cooked by someone's tired hands, paid for with someone's work. All true. And the prayer still calls it a gift, from God, before it's anything else. It quietly rearranges the plate. Third, which we are about to receive. Receive, not take. You can't earn a gift; you can only accept it. And from thy bounty: from God's generosity, which is bigger than this meal. Fourth, through Christ our Lord. The prayer goes through Jesus, who did this himself. In Mark's Gospel, a huge hungry crowd has followed him into a deserted place, and the disciples want to send them away to buy food. Instead he takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the loaves, and gives them to be shared. Everyone eats. Some readers see grace at the table as copying that gesture: look up, bless, then share. Some families add grace after meals too, a short thanks when the plates are empty. Before or after, the point is the same. The food was a gift.

1392.title: Blessing children
1392.hook: a parent traces a cross on a child's forehead at night
1392.howItsDone: Some Catholic parents bless their children each night, or as they leave the house, by tracing a small sign of the cross on the forehead with a thumb, sometimes with holy water or a few words. The custom echoes the cross the priest, parents and godparents trace on the child's forehead at baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace before meals: a few words said over a plate before the first bite. Your line was these thy gifts.

Lights out. The story is finished, the water glass is on the nightstand, and a small voice has asked for one more thing and been told no. The parent leans down in the dark and, with a thumb, draws a small cross on the child's forehead. Down, then across. Sometimes with a few words, sometimes none. The child is often half asleep and doesn't notice. Years later, that child is a teenager walking out the door with car keys, and the parent's thumb still finds the forehead on the way out. Where does a habit like that come from? Further back than bedtime.
screen: `LIGHTS OUT. A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `DOWN, THEN ACROSS.` → `WHERE DOES IT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Start in Mark's Gospel. People are bringing children to Jesus, and the disciples try to send them away. Jesus is indignant: let the little children come. Then Mark slows down, in the Douay-Rheims: "And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them." Not a lesson. Not a test. Arms, hands, and a blessing. Next, where the cross on the forehead comes from. At an infant's baptism, before the water, the priest or deacon welcomes the child and traces the sign of the cross on the forehead, claiming the child for Christ. Then the rite invites the parents and godparents to do the same. So the first cross on that forehead is made by the Church, and the next ones by the people who will raise the child. The bedtime cross is the baptism cross, repeated. Then, the parent's part. The Church's book of blessings includes blessings that parents themselves may lead for their children. The thumb at bedtime isn't borrowing anyone's job; it's finishing what the parents were invited to begin at the font. Last, what it's for. Catholic parents who bless their children at night are handing them back, for the hours they can't watch over them, to the one they believe is always watching. It's also a way to end a hard day well. Whatever the argument was about at dinner, the last word of the day is a blessing.

1393.title: Eternal rest
1393.hook: eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord
1393.howItsDone: Catholics say the Eternal Rest prayer for the dead at funerals, at graves, during November, after grace or the rosary, and whenever a person who has died is remembered. It is often printed on the back of funeral prayer cards.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing children: a parent's thumb drawing a small cross before sleep. Your line was a cross on the forehead.

A small card, the size of a playing card, left on a table at the back of a funeral home. On the front, a painting of Jesus or Mary. On the back, a name, two dates, and four short lines. People slip these cards into wallets, Bibles and kitchen drawers, and find them years later, a little bent at the corners. The four lines are often the same, whoever's name is above them. Catholics say them for the famous and the forgotten alike.
screen: `A CARD AT THE BACK OF THE FUNERAL HOME.` → `A NAME, TWO DATES, FOUR LINES.` → `THE SAME LINES FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in traditional English. "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen." In Latin the prayer opens "Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine." Requiem is the Latin for rest. Those words also open the entrance chant of the Church's Mass for the dead, which is why that Mass, and music written for it, carry the name requiem. The prayer asks two gifts. Rest, after a life of work and worry. And light after the dark of death: perpetual light, light that doesn't go out. It asks nothing for the person saying it; it's entirely for someone else. Why pray for the dead at all? You met the answer in year two, in the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has prayers and sacrifice offered for fallen soldiers. The Douay-Rheims closes the passage: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins." The Catechism teaches that those who die in God's friendship but still need purifying can be helped by the prayers of the living. Not every church counts Maccabees as scripture, or prays for the dead in this way, and that difference can be named plainly. Last, look back at this week: pilgrims at Lourdes and Fatima, a local shrine, the incorruptibles, a votive candle, grace before meals, a cross on a child's forehead. Again and again, someone was held up to God. Today's prayer is the same gesture, for people who can no longer ask for anything themselves.
screen: `REQUIEM IS THE LATIN FOR REST.` · `REST AND LIGHT, ASKED FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `A WEEK OF HOLDING PEOPLE UP.` · then, large: `LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.`

segments.voice: Let one name come to mind, someone who has died: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, someone you barely knew but haven't forgotten. If you pray, say the four lines for them, then let another name come, and another; if you don't, say each name and leave a breath of quiet after it, like a candle left burning. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Requiem. Latin for rest, the first word of the Church's prayer for the dead and of the entrance chant at a Mass for the dead. Today's word.
Your line: let perpetual light shine. Rest, and a light that doesn't go out. See you tomorrow.
